To estimate the causal effect of rural income growth on Hindu-Muslim riots, an instrumental variables strategy is required because rural income growth is likely endogenous to local conflict and unobserved economic shocks. I evaluated two potential instruments in the dataset—`monsoon_dev` and `works_draw`—and concluded that neither provides a credible basis for identification. Although `monsoon_dev` strongly predicts rural income growth conditional on district and year fixed effects, it violates the exclusion restriction: in deficit monsoon years (`monsoon_dev` below -10 percent), state relief rules redeploy reserve police battalions from rural stations to district headquarters to guard relief stores, directly altering local policing capacity and riot dynamics. The alternative candidate, `works_draw`, is randomly assigned and satisfies the exclusion restriction, but it is only available for 16 districts over three years and suffers from a severely weak first stage ($F \approx 2$). Because one candidate is invalid and the other is too weak and limited in coverage for reliable inference, the dataset does not support a credible instrumental variables design. I therefore recommend against proceeding with an IV estimation using these variables, or else restricting use of `monsoon_dev` to above-threshold variation only if external evidence confirms police redeployments never occur above the -10 percent cutoff.

CANDIDATES:
monsoon_dev | violated
works_draw | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: NONE

There is no credible instrumental variable in this dataset to estimate the causal effect of rural income growth on Hindu-Muslim riots. The first candidate instrument, `monsoon_dev` (percent deviation of monsoon rainfall from its historical average), has a strong first stage on rural income growth within a district and year fixed-effects framework. However, `monsoon_dev` violates the exclusion restriction because below-average monsoon rainfall automatically triggers state relief rules that redeploy reserve police battalions from rural stations to district headquarters, directly affecting policing presence and the likelihood or reporting of riots. The second candidate, `works_draw` (the 1992 random lottery for a rural public-works program), satisfies independence and the exclusion restriction, as it was randomly assigned and changed nothing else in the drawn districts. Unfortunately, `works_draw` is only defined for 16 districts in a single state from 1993–1995 (48 district-year observations) and suffers from a severely weak first stage (F-statistic of about 2), making instrumental-variables estimation unreliable. Therefore, I recommend against an IV strategy with the current variables; the best available options are a reduced-form intent-to-treat analysis of `works_draw` in the 16-district subsample or a two-way fixed effects panel regression with baseline controls (`pop_1981`, `muslim_share`, `urban_share`, `literacy`, `riots_prev`), while acknowledging that time-varying unobserved shocks remain a threat to identification.

Neither candidate instrument in the dataset supports a credible instrumental variables strategy to estimate the causal effect of rural income growth on Hindu-Muslim riots. The monsoon rainfall variable (`monsoon_dev`) violates the exclusion restriction because below-average rainfall triggers state relief rules that redeploy reserve police battalions from rural stations to district headquarters, directly affecting policing and riot counts independently of rural income. The public-works lottery variable (`works_draw`) satisfies randomization and exclusion, but it is only defined for 16 districts in 1993–1995 and suffers from a severe weak-instrument problem with a first-stage F-statistic of about 2. Because no valid and sufficiently strong instrument is available, we must rely on a two-way fixed effects panel regression of district-year riots on rural income growth, controlling for district and year fixed effects or interactions of year indicators with baseline 1981 covariates (`pop_1981`, `muslim_share`, `urban_share`, `literacy`, and `riots_prev`). Alternatively, `works_draw` can only be used for a reduced-form intent-to-treat analysis of the public-works program in that single state, which remains severely underpowered. The main threat to identification in the panel specification is time-varying unobserved confounding—such as local political shocks or price and policing changes—that simultaneously affects district rural income growth and communal violence.

The second candidate, `works_draw`, satisfies random assignment and the exclusion restriction, but it is only defined for 16 districts over three years (48 observations) and suffers from severe weak-instrument bias with a first-stage F-statistic of about 2. Instead, we can only estimate the reduced-form intent-to-treat effect of `works_draw` on riots within the 16-district experimental subsample (controlling for 1981 baseline characteristics `pop_1981`, `muslim_share`, `urban_share`, `literacy`, and `riots_prev`), or use two-way fixed effects as a descriptive analysis while acknowledging the threat of time-varying unobserved confounders.

This dataset does not support a credible instrumental-variables strategy because neither candidate instrument satisfies both relevance and exclusion. First, `monsoon_dev` (monsoon rainfall deviation) strongly predicts rural income growth, but it violates the exclusion restriction because deficit monsoon years (`monsoon_dev` below -10 percent) automatically trigger relief rules that redeploy reserve police battalions from rural stations to district headquarters, directly altering riot deterrence and policing capacity. Second, `works_draw` (the 1992 public-works lottery) satisfies exogeneity and exclusion, but it is only defined for 16 districts in one state during 1993–1995 and suffers from a weak first stage (F-statistic of about 2), which would yield severely biased and imprecise two-stage least squares estimates. Given the failure of both instruments, the most transparent fallback is a two-way fixed effects panel regression of district-year Hindu-Muslim riots on rural income growth, including district and year fixed effects as well as interactions between year indicators and 1981 baseline covariates (`pop_1981`, `muslim_share`, `urban_share`, `literacy`, and `riots_prev`). If one attempts to salvage `monsoon_dev` by restricting variation to above-threshold rainfall (`monsoon_dev` $\ge -10$) while controlling for a deficit-year indicator, the design still faces the threat of unmeasured rainfall channels or sample selection. Ultimately, without a valid and strong instrument, the main threat to identification is time-varying omitted variables and reverse causality between communal violence and local economic activity.

Neither candidate instrument in the dataset provides a credible instrumental-variables design to estimate the causal effect of rural income growth on Hindu-Muslim riots. The first candidate, `monsoon_dev` (monsoon rainfall deviation), violates the exclusion restriction because rainfall deficits below -10 percent trigger relief rules that redeploy reserve police battalions from rural stations to district headquarters, directly affecting riot deterrence and police-based riot reporting independent of income growth. The second candidate, `works_draw` (the 1992 public-works lottery), satisfies exogeneity and exclusion by construction, but suffers from severe weak-instrument bias (first-stage F-statistic of about 2) and is only defined for 16 districts in a single state from 1993 to 1995. Because no valid and sufficiently strong instrument is available across the sample, we cannot credibly identify the causal effect using two-stage least squares. Instead, we can only estimate descriptive panel regressions of riots on rural income growth with district and year fixed effects—or interact `monsoon_dev` above the -10 percent threshold if the policy rule is strictly binding, though weather still poses direct physiological and logistical threats to riot participation—while transparently reporting that endogeneity and omitted time-varying shocks remain unresolved threats to causal inference.

To estimate the causal effect of voter turnout on the incumbent party's presidential vote share, we cannot rely on the full-sample election-day rainfall instrument (`eday_rain`) because a 1952 law moved polling places on wet election days (>0.1 inches of rain) into county courthouses where the incumbent party's campaign posters remained on display, directly violating the exclusion restriction. Instead, we will use an instrumental variables strategy restricted to the 180 county-elections in the 1996–2000 three-state pilot, instrumenting county turnout with `reminder_draw`, the random assignment of a nonpartisan mailed election reminder. Because `reminder_draw` was randomly assigned, named no candidate or party, and changed nothing else in drawn counties, it satisfies independence and the exclusion restriction. We will include state and election-year fixed effects along with pre-treatment county covariates (`dem_prev`, `pop_density`, `pct_rural`, `median_inc`) to improve precision. The main threat to this design is weak-instrument bias—since `reminder_draw` raises turnout by only 0.3 percentage points with a first-stage F-statistic of about 4—as well as limited external validity from restricting the analysis to the 180 pilot county-elections. To address the weak first stage, we will report Anderson-Rubin weak-instrument-robust confidence intervals alongside two-stage least squares estimates.

CANDIDATES:
eday_rain | violated
reminder_draw | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: reminder_draw

We cannot credibly estimate the causal effect using standard instrumental variables across the full panel because neither candidate instrument in the dataset satisfies both validity and strength requirements. The first candidate, election-day rainfall (`eday_rain`), violates the exclusion restriction because a 1952 law moved polling places on rainy days into county courthouses where the incumbent party's campaign posters remained on display, creating a direct channel to the incumbent's vote share. The second candidate, the randomized nonpartisan voter reminder (`reminder_draw`), satisfies independence and exclusion, but it is only available for 180 county-elections in a 1996–2000 pilot and suffers from a weak first stage ($F \approx 4$). Consequently, for the 180-observation pilot subsample, we can at best report weak-IV-robust Anderson–Rubin confidence sets using `reminder_draw` as an instrument for turnout, controlling for state-by-year fixed effects and baseline covariates (`dem_prev`, `pop_density`, `pct_rural`, `median_inc`). For the full 1948–2000 panel, we must fall back on a two-way fixed effects regression of incumbent vote share on county turnout with county and state-by-election-year fixed effects plus time-varying controls (`dem_prev`, `pop_density`, `pct_rural`, `median_inc`). The main threat to identification is that the pilot subsample is too underpowered for precise inference, while the full-sample panel estimates remain vulnerable to time-varying unobserved county shocks—such as local campaign mobilization or ballot initiatives—that simultaneously drive turnout and incumbent support.

CANDIDATES:
eday_rain | violated
reminder_draw | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: NONE

To estimate the causal effect of county voter turnout on the incumbent president's party vote share, we evaluate an instrumental variables (IV) strategy alongside a two-way fixed effects panel design using county and election-year fixed effects and baseline covariates (`dem_prev`, `pop_density`, `pct_rural`, `median_inc`). The first candidate instrument, election-day rainfall (`eday_rain`), strongly predicts turnout (-1.1 percentage points per inch) conditional on county and year fixed effects. However, `eday_rain` violates the exclusion restriction because a 1952 state law moved polling places on rainy election days into county courthouses where the incumbent party's campaign posters remained on display, directly affecting the incumbent's vote share. The second candidate instrument, `reminder_draw`, exploits a randomized nonpartisan mailed reminder pilot across 180 county-elections in three states from 1996 to 2000, which satisfies random assignment and the exclusion restriction. However, `reminder_draw` is a doubtful instrument because it is severely underpowered, with only 180 observations, a small first-stage effect (0.3 percentage points), and a weak first-stage F-statistic of about 4 that would induce severe weak-instrument bias in standard 2SLS. Consequently, no valid and strong instrument is available in the dataset, and any IV analysis restricted to the `reminder_draw` pilot subsample would have to rely on weak-instrument-robust inference (such as Anderson-Rubin confidence intervals) while facing limited external validity.

CANDIDATES:
eday_rain | violated
reminder_draw | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: NONE

We cannot credibly estimate the causal effect of county turnout on the incumbent party's vote share across the full sample using standard instrumental variables because neither candidate instrument in the dataset satisfies all requirements for valid, strong identification. The classic election-day rainfall instrument (`eday_rain`) violates the exclusion restriction: election days with over 0.1 inches of rain were logged as wet polling days, which under a 1952 law moved voting into county courthouses where the incumbent party's campaign posters remained on display, directly affecting the incumbent vote share outside of turnout. The randomized mailed-reminder pilot (`reminder_draw`) satisfies independence and exclusion because it was randomly assigned and nonpartisan, and could in principle be used in an instrumental variables specification controlling for `state` and election-year fixed effects along with baseline county covariates (`dem_prev`, `pop_density`, `pct_rural`, `median_inc`, `south`). However, `reminder_draw` is available for only 180 county-elections in three states from 1996 to 2000 and suffers from a weak first stage ($F \approx 4$), making standard two-stage least squares biased and unreliable. The main threat to identification is therefore weak-instrument bias and severe lack of statistical power in the `reminder_draw` subsample alongside the direct courthouse-poster exclusion violation for `eday_rain`. Consequently, we should not rely on either variable for a standard 2SLS design, and any exploratory analysis restricted to the 180-observation `reminder_draw` pilot must rely strictly on weak-instrument-robust Anderson–Rubin confidence intervals rather than point estimates.

eday_rain | violated
reminder_draw | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: NONE

We do not have a credible instrumental-variables strategy in the full dataset to estimate the causal effect of county voter turnout on the incumbent party's vote share. The standard candidate instrument, election-day rainfall (`eday_rain`), violates the exclusion restriction because a 1952 law moved polling places on wet polling days (over 0.1 inches of rain) into county courthouses where the incumbent party's campaign posters remained on display, directly affecting the incumbent vote share. The alternative candidate instrument, the randomized nonpartisan mailed reminder (`reminder_draw`), satisfies random assignment and exclusion but is only available for a 180-observation pilot from 1996–2000 and suffers from a weak first stage ($F \approx 4$). If we restrict attention to the 180-observation pilot, we could report Anderson-Rubin weak-instrument-robust confidence intervals using `reminder_draw` (controlling for `state` and baseline covariates like `dem_prev`, `pop_density`, `pct_rural`, and `median_inc`), though statistical power will be severely limited and external validity to the full 1948–2000 sample will be questionable. In the full sample, any two-way fixed effects or selection-on-observables regression controlling for county and year fixed effects and baseline covariates faces the central threat of time-varying unobserved county shocks—such as local campaign intensity or candidate appeal—that simultaneously drive both turnout and support for the incumbent party. Consequently, I recommend against relying on either instrument for a point-identified 2SLS estimate and instead suggest reporting the reduced-form intent-to-treat effect of `reminder_draw` alongside weak-IV bounds in the pilot subsample.

Neither candidate instrument in the dataset supports a credible instrumental-variables estimate across the study sample, so I recommend against proceeding with standard 2SLS on the full panel. The traditional election-day rainfall instrument (`eday_rain`) violates the exclusion restriction because a 1952 state law moved polling places on rainy days into county courthouses where the incumbent party's campaign posters remained on display, creating a direct channel to the incumbent's vote share. The randomized nonpartisan mailer (`reminder_draw`) satisfies random assignment and exclusion—it named no party or candidate and changed nothing else—but it is available for only 180 county-elections in a 1996–2000 three-state pilot and has a weak first stage ($F \approx 4$, raising turnout by 0.3 percentage points). If we restrict analysis to the 180 pilot county-elections, we can report the reduced-form intent-to-treat effect of `reminder_draw` on incumbent vote share and construct weak-instrument-robust Anderson–Rubin confidence sets, controlling for baseline covariates (`dem_prev`, `pop_density`, `pct_rural`, `median_inc`) and state-by-year fixed effects. For the full 1948–2000 panel (or pre-1952 elections before the courthouse law took effect), a two-way fixed effects regression with county and election-year fixed effects and time-varying controls is the only available fallback, though it remains vulnerable to unobserved time-varying county shocks that jointly affect turnout and incumbent support. Consequently, the main threat to identification is the direct courthouse-poster effect for `eday_rain` and severe weak-instrument bias and limited external validity for `reminder_draw`.

Neither candidate instrument in the dataset supports a credible standard instrumental-variables design across the full sample. The `waterways` variable (following Ananat 2011) violates the exclusion restriction here because state law requires cities to pay an annual flood-control maintenance levy from their general budget for each crossing waterway, directly raising direct general expenditure per resident. The `audit_grant` indicator is randomly assigned and satisfies the exclusion restriction since the funds went to nonprofits rather than city budgets, but it is available for only 40 cities and suffers from a severe weak-instrument problem (first-stage F-statistic of about 2). Consequently, rather than relying on an invalid full-sample IV, I recommend estimating a panel two-way fixed effects model—regressing per-capita direct general expenditure on the multigroup entropy segregation index with city and state-by-year fixed effects, controlling for `log_pop`, `pct_black`, `pct_hisp`, `med_income`, and `own_rate`. As a supplementary check on the 40-city experimental subsample, we can report reduced-form intent-to-treat estimates and Anderson-Rubin weak-instrument-robust confidence intervals using `audit_grant` interacted with post-1990 indicators. The main threat to the panel strategy is time-varying unobserved city-level shocks, such as local economic or fiscal crises, that simultaneously drive residential sorting and municipal spending.

INSTRUMENT: NONE

Because the dataset lacks a valid and strong instrumental variable, I recommend a panel two-way fixed effects strategy rather than an instrumental-variables design. Specifically, neither candidate instrument in the codebook is suitable: `waterways` violates the exclusion restriction because state law mandates annual flood-control maintenance payments from the city's general budget for each waterway (directly affecting direct general expenditure), while `audit_grant` is only available for 40 cities after 1990 and suffers from severe weak-instrument bias (first-stage F-statistic of about 2). Instead, we should regress city direct general expenditure per resident on the multigroup entropy segregation index, including city fixed effects to absorb time-invariant municipal characteristics (such as baseline geography and `waterways`) and region-by-year or state-by-year fixed effects to absorb common shocks across the 1980, 1990, 2000, and 2010 census waves. To account for observable demographic and economic sorting, the specification should control for time-varying city characteristics: `log_pop`, `pct_black`, `pct_hisp`, `med_income`, and `own_rate`. We can also report weak-instrument-robust Anderson-Rubin confidence intervals for the `audit_grant` subsample only as a supplementary check, though it will lack statistical power. The main threat to identification in the panel design is time-varying unobserved confounding—such as local fiscal crises, Tiebout sorting on public goods, or unobserved neighborhood policy shifts—that simultaneously alters residential segregation and municipal spending within cities over time.

waterways | violated
audit_grant | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: NONE

Because the available dataset lacks a valid and strong instrumental variable, I plan to estimate the effect of racial segregation on per-capita direct general expenditure using a panel two-way fixed effects design with city and state-by-year (or region-by-year) fixed effects. We will regress city direct general expenditure per resident on the multigroup entropy segregation index, controlling for time-varying demographic and economic covariates (`log_pop`, `pct_black`, `pct_hisp`, `med_income`, and `own_rate`). I considered `waterways` (the number of rivers and streams crossing the city) as a potential Ananat-style instrument for segregation, but it violates the exclusion restriction because state law requires cities to pay an annual flood-control maintenance levy per waterway directly from their general budget. I also considered `audit_grant` (the 1990 random draw for fair-housing testing grants), which satisfies independence and exclusion because the funds went to nonprofits rather than city governments, but it is only defined for 40 cities and suffers from a weak first stage ($F \approx 2$). Consequently, relying on within-city variation over the 1980–2010 census waves rather than instrumental variables is the most defensible approach with these data. The main threat to this panel strategy is time-varying unobserved confounding—such as local fiscal shocks, Tiebout sorting, or political shifts—that simultaneously alters residential segregation and municipal spending decisions.

INSTRUMENT: NONE

To estimate the causal effect of racial residential segregation on city direct general expenditure per resident, I recommend a panel two-way fixed-effects specification rather than an instrumental-variables design because neither candidate instrument in the dataset is credible. The classic Hoxby-style instrument, `waterways`, violates the exclusion restriction because state law requires cities to pay an annual flood-control maintenance levy from their general budget for each 1920 boundary stream that crosses the city, directly shifting general expenditure. The randomized `audit_grant` satisfies independence and exclusion—since the grant went to nonprofits rather than city budgets and changed nothing else—but it is available for only 40 cities and suffers from severe weak-instrument bias with a first-stage F-statistic of about 2. Instead, we can exploit the four-decade panel (1980, 1990, 2000, and 2010) by regressing per-resident direct general expenditure on the multigroup entropy segregation index while including city fixed effects and state-by-year (or region-by-year) fixed effects. To absorb time-varying demographic and economic confounding, we will control for `log_pop`, `pct_black`, `pct_hisp`, `med_income`, and `own_rate`. The main threat to identification in this panel design is time-varying unobserved confounding—such as unobserved local political shifts or fiscal shocks—that simultaneously alters residential sorting and municipal spending decisions within a city over time.

To estimate the causal effect of racial segregation (the multigroup entropy index) on direct general expenditure per resident, I evaluated an instrumental variables strategy using the two candidate instruments in the dataset alongside controls such as `log_pop`, `pct_black`, `pct_hisp`, `med_income`, `own_rate`, and `region`. The first candidate instrument, `waterways` (the number of 1920 boundary streams crossing the city), strongly predicts segregation conditional on log population and state-by-year fixed effects. However, the program documentation reveals that state law requires cities to pay an annual flood-control maintenance levy from their general budget for each 1920 boundary stream, which directly affects general expenditure and violates the exclusion restriction. The second candidate, `audit_grant` (a 1990 randomized fair-housing audit grant to nonprofits), satisfies random assignment and the exclusion restriction because it bypassed city budgets and changed nothing else in drawn cities. Nevertheless, `audit_grant` is only defined for 40 cities and has a first-stage F-statistic of about 2, making it far too weak to support credible estimation. Because neither instrument is both valid and sufficiently strong, the dataset cannot support a credible instrumental variables design, leaving selection on unobservables as the main threat to any panel fixed-effects or covariate-adjusted regression.

Neither candidate instrument in the dataset supports a credible instrumental-variables design for estimating the causal effect of racial segregation on city direct general expenditure per resident. The Cutler-Glaeser-style instrument `waterways` is invalid because every counted waterway is a 1920 boundary stream, and state law requires cities to pay an annual flood-control maintenance levy from their general budget for each such stream, directly shifting the public spending outcome and violating the exclusion restriction. The randomized fair-housing grant indicator (`audit_grant`) satisfies exogeneity and exclusion because it funded non-governmental nonprofits and changed nothing else in the city, but it is only defined for 40 large cities and suffers from severe weak-instrument bias with a first-stage F-statistic of about 2. Without a valid and strong instrument, the best available fallback is a two-way fixed-effects panel regression across the 1980–2010 census waves that includes city and state-by-year fixed effects while controlling for time-varying covariates (`log_pop`, `pct_black`, `pct_hisp`, `med_income`, and `own_rate`). However, this panel approach is not a quasi-experimental design and remains vulnerable to time-varying unobserved confounders—such as local economic shocks, suburbanization dynamics, or fiscal crises—that simultaneously reshape residential sorting and municipal budgets.

Because neither candidate instrument in the dataset supports a credible instrumental-variables design, I recommend not using an IV strategy. The first candidate, `season_rain`, has a strong effect on log household income, but it violates the exclusion restriction because above-average rainfall made village roads impassable and caused the regional health office to suspend mobile clinic rounds for three months, directly affecting illness episodes independently of household income (as well as potentially changing disease ecology directly). The second candidate, `transfer_draw`, comes from a randomized cash transfer lottery across 6 pilot villages and satisfies exogeneity and the exclusion restriction, but it is only defined for 6 of the 51 villages and suffers from severe weak-instrument problems (an average log income effect of 0.02 and a first-stage F-statistic of about 2). Using `transfer_draw` in two-stage least squares would yield severely biased and uninformative estimates, though we can still report the reduced-form intent-to-treat effect of `transfer_draw` on illness episodes in the 6 pilot villages using a difference-in-differences specification. For the full sample, the best available specification is a panel fixed-effects regression of illness episodes on log household income per adult equivalent, controlling for individual and survey-round fixed effects alongside time-varying covariates (`age`, `hh_size`, `land_acres`, and `season_rain`). The main threat to this panel strategy is time-varying unobserved confounding and reverse causality, such as acute health shocks simultaneously increasing illness episodes and reducing household labor income between survey rounds.

season_rain | violated
transfer_draw | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: NONE

An instrumental variables strategy is the natural approach to address reverse causality and unobserved confounding between log household income per adult equivalent and reported illness episodes, so I evaluated the two potential instruments in the dataset: `season_rain` and `transfer_draw`. Using `season_rain` (with individual and survey-round fixed effects) violates the exclusion restriction because wet seasons (>100 mm deviation) directly affect health by triggering the three-month suspension of mobile clinic rounds due to impassable roads, as well as potentially altering disease environments directly. Conversely, while `transfer_draw` satisfies the exclusion restriction because the 1993 unconditional cash transfer lottery was randomized and changed nothing else in the drawn villages, it is only defined for 6 of the 51 villages and suffers from a severe weak-instrument problem (first-stage F-statistic of about 2). Because standard two-stage least squares with `transfer_draw` would be severely biased and underpowered, we cannot rely on a conventional IV point estimate from either candidate. Instead, I recommend reporting reduced-form (intent-to-treat) and weak-instrument-robust (e.g., Anderson-Rubin) confidence intervals on the 6-village pilot subsample using `transfer_draw` and survey-round/individual fixed effects, supplemented by a panel fixed-effects regression on the full 51-village sample controlling for `age`, `female`, `educ_years`, `hh_size`, `dist_clinic`, and `land_acres`. The main threat to identification is that the 6-village experimental subsample lacks statistical power to detect meaningful effects, while the full-sample panel fixed-effects estimates remain vulnerable to time-varying unobserved shocks—such as acute health shocks that simultaneously increase illness episodes and reduce household labor income.

Specifically, `season_rain` violates the exclusion restriction because above-average rainfall caused the regional health office to suspend mobile clinic rounds for three months (and rainfall directly alters vector-borne disease risk), directly affecting illness episodes outside of household income. Meanwhile, `transfer_draw` is only defined for a 6-village pilot subsample and suffers from a severe weak-instrument problem, with a first-stage F-statistic of only about 2. Because no valid and strong instrument is available for the study sample, we should instead estimate a two-way fixed effects panel regression of illness episodes on log household income per adult equivalent, including individual and survey-round fixed effects alongside time-varying controls such as `age` and `hh_size` (and controlling for `season_rain` to block the weather and clinic-access confounding path). For the 6 pilot villages, we can separately report the reduced-form intent-to-treat effect of `transfer_draw` interacted with post-1993 indicators, or use weak-instrument-robust inference (such as Anderson-Rubin confidence intervals), while acknowledging that it will be imprecise. The main threat to the panel fixed-effects strategy is time-varying unobserved confounding and reverse causality, such as acute health shocks simultaneously increasing illness episodes and reducing household labor income between survey rounds.

To estimate the causal effect of log household income per adult equivalent on reported illness episodes, we cannot rely on standard instrumental variables because neither candidate instrument in the dataset is both valid and sufficiently strong. First, `season_rain` (rainfall deviation) violates the exclusion restriction because above-average rainfall caused the regional health office to suspend mobile clinic rounds for three months due to impassable roads—directly affecting health and healthcare access independently of household income (in addition to any direct biological effects of rain on vector- and water-borne disease). Second, while `transfer_draw` (the 1993 random cash-transfer lottery across the six pilot villages) satisfies randomization and exclusion, it is only defined for a six-village subsample and suffers from severe weak-instrument bias with a first-stage F-statistic of about 2 (raising log income by only 0.02). The main threat to identification in the panel fixed-effects specification is time-varying unobserved confounding and reverse causality, such as acute health shocks that simultaneously increase illness episodes and reduce contemporaneous labor supply and household income.

As a fallback, we can estimate two-way fixed effects regressions (controlling for individual and survey-round fixed effects as well as time-varying covariates like `age` and `hh_size`) or report the reduced-form intent-to-treat effect of `transfer_draw` in the pilot villages. The main threat to the panel fixed-effects approach is time-varying unobserved confounding and reverse causality, such as acute health shocks simultaneously increasing illness episodes and reducing household labor income.
